about.title: Los Banos Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Los Banos sees steady foot traffic through its shopping centers, restaurants, and public buildings, many clustered near Rt 152 and Pacheco Boulevard. Wet floors, uneven pavement, poor lighting in a parking lot, or a spill left unattended can turn an ordinary errand into a painful injury. California law doesn't automatically hold a property owner responsible just because someone got hurt on their premises — you generally have to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn people about it. That's why what happens right after a fall matters: photos of the scene, names of witnesses, and any store surveillance footage can make a real difference later. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself, but we can connect you, at no cost, with an independent attorney in Merced County who understands how these claims work and can help you sort out next steps.

whyChoose.title: Why Documentation Matters in Los Banos Premises Cases

items.title: Notice Is the Whole Case
items.desc: Under California law, you generally have to show the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can help track down maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that speak to that.

items.title: Surveillance Video Disappears Fast
items.desc: Many Los Banos businesses overwrite security footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference between having proof and having none.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for not seeing a hazard, you may still recover a reduced amount rather than nothing at all.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Los Banos?
items.answer: In California, you generally have two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit for injuries. That window can be much shorter if the property involved is owned by a government entity, like a city building or public sidewalk, so it's worth checking sooner rather than later.

items.question: What if I fell in a store parking lot near Rt 152 or Pacheco Boulevard?
items.answer: Parking lots, sidewalks, and entryways are common trouble spots because of uneven pavement, potholes, or poor lighting. Ownership and maintenance responsibility can get complicated when multiple businesses share a lot, so an attorney can help figure out who's accountable.

items.question: Do I need proof the store knew about the hazard?
items.answer: Generally, yes — California law requires showing the owner had notice of the dangerous condition, either because they created it, knew about it, or should have discovered it through reasonable inspection. Evidence like how long a spill sat there or prior complaints can help establish that.
